clinicalPearls: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes (APS) are divided into two principal categories: APS type 1 (APS-1) and APS type 2 (APS-2); some authors further split APS-2 into APS-3 and APS-4, but this added subdivision adds little to understanding pathogenesis or guiding management (Harrison 22e p.3089).

Although the underlying autoimmunity predominantly targets endocrine glands, many nonendocrine tissues can be affected, so a range of nonendocrine disorders is recognized as part of these syndromes (Harrison 22e p.3089).

APS-1 (APECED) is defined by a triad of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison's disease; the diagnosis is usually made clinically when two of these three major components are present (Harrison 22e p.3089).

APS-1 is rare (<500 reported cases) and classically is autosomal recessive, caused by mutations in the AIRE gene on chromosome 21; AIRE is most highly expressed in thymic medullary epithelial cells where it drives expression of tissue-specific self-antigens such as insulin (Harrison 22e p.3089).

Anticytokine autoantibodies are characteristic of APS-1: anti-IL-17A, anti-IL-17F, and anti-IL-22 underlie the mucocutaneous candidiasis, while detection of anti-interferon alpha and anti-interferon omega antibodies identifies nearly 100% of APS-1 cases and is not seen in other autoimmune disorders (Harrison 22e p.3089-3090).

APS-1 typically begins in infancy with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (mouth and nails more than skin/esophagus), followed by hypoparathyroidism (>85% of cases) and then Addison's disease (nearly 80%); the interval between components can be many years and the order is variable (Harrison 22e p.3089-3090).

APS-2 is more common (prevalence 1-2 per 100,000), shows a female predominance (at least 3:1), has multigenerational inheritance, and usually presents in adulthood with peak incidence between 20 and 60 years (Harrison 22e p.3090).

APS-2 is defined by two or more of: primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease, 50-70%), Graves' disease or autoimmune thyroiditis (15-69%), type 1 diabetes (40-50%), and primary hypogonadism; associated conditions include celiac disease, myasthenia gravis, vitiligo, alopecia, serositis, and pernicious anemia (Harrison 22e p.3090).

Adrenal insufficiency can be masked by coexisting primary hypothyroidism because low thyroid hormone prolongs the half-life of cortisol; patients with hypothyroidism and possible APS should be screened for adrenal insufficiency, since starting thyroid hormone first can precipitate an adrenal crisis (Harrison 22e p.3090).

Antibody screening can detect risk years before clinical disease: anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies are highly predictive of future adrenal insufficiency, and presence of two or more islet autoantibodies with normal glucose tolerance is defined as stage 1 type 1 diabetes with a near-100% lifetime risk of clinical disease (Harrison 22e p.3091).

About 50% of patients with Addison's disease develop another autoimmune disorder during their lifetime, so a new diagnosis of Addison's should prompt broader screening for linked conditions (Harrison 22e p.3091).
harrison.pathophysiology: APS-1 is a monogenic, classically autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the AIRE (autoimmune regulator) gene on chromosome 21. AIRE is most highly expressed in thymic medullary epithelial cells, where it promotes expression of tissue-specific self-antigens; its loss reduces this expression and is thought to allow autoreactive T cells to escape central (thymic) deletion. Over 100 mutations are described, with higher frequency in certain ethnic groups (Iranian Jews, Sardinians, Finns, Norwegians, Irish). Newly recognized autosomal dominant mutations cluster in the PHD1 domain and tend to cause later-onset, less aggressive disease. Patients develop anticytokine autoantibodies (anti-IL-17A, IL-17F, IL-22, and type 1 interferons). In contrast, APS-2 is polygenic, with the dominant risk in the HLA complex on chromosome 6: Addison's disease in APS-2 is strongly linked to HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4, with additional contributions from HLA-B8, DQ2, DQ8, and DRB1 subtypes. Non-HLA immune genes including MIC-A (the 5.1 allele strongly associated with Addison's), PTPN22, CTLA4, and IL-2R-alpha variants further modulate susceptibility. Organ damage in both syndromes is mediated by organ-specific autoantibodies and autoreactive T cells against targets such as 21-hydroxylase, GAD65, thyroid peroxidase, transglutaminase, and intrinsic factor (Harrison 22e p.3089-3091).
additionalDifferentials: Isolated autoimmune Addison's disease without polyglandular involvement
Isolated autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis or Graves' disease
Adult combined pituitary hormone deficiency with anti-Pit1 autoantibodies (anti-Pit1 syndrome)
Kearns-Sayre and DIDMOAD (Wolfram) syndromes as causes of multiple endocrine deficiencies
infectionMimics: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis from primary immunodeficiencies other than APS-1 (e.g., STAT1 gain-of-function)
Congenital rubella associated with thyroiditis and/or diabetes
nonInfectiousMimics: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced endocrinopathies producing multiple gland failure
Sequential isolated autoimmune endocrinopathies occurring by chance
Trisomy 21 and Turner's syndrome associated autoimmune endocrine disease
additionalInvestigations: AIRE gene sequencing in suspected APS-1
Anti-interferon alpha and anti-interferon omega antibodies (identify nearly 100% of APS-1)
Anticytokine antibodies to IL-17 and IL-22 (support candidiasis of APS-1)
Anti-21-hydroxylase (and anti-17-hydroxylase) autoantibodies for Addison's disease risk
Morning ACTH and cortisol; cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test if abnormal
Serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH for hypoparathyroidism
TSH with anti-TPO/anti-thyroglobulin and anti-TSH receptor antibodies
Islet autoantibodies (insulin, GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8) and hemoglobin A1c for type 1 diabetes
Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies for celiac disease
Vitamin B12, CBC, and anti-parietal cell/intrinsic factor antibodies for pernicious anemia
Peripheral blood smear for Howell-Jolly bodies to detect asplenism (with splenic ultrasound if positive)
redFlags: New thyroid hormone replacement in an undiagnosed patient with adrenal insufficiency can precipitate an adrenal crisis
Treatment of mucocutaneous candidiasis with ketoconazole in a patient with subclinical adrenal insufficiency may also precipitate adrenal crisis
Hyperpigmentation, unexplained hyponatremia/hyperkalemia, or hypotension signaling evolving Addison's disease
Tetany or seizures from hypocalcemia indicating hypoparathyroidism
Howell-Jolly bodies on smear indicating functional asplenism and increased infection risk in APS-1
Refractory diarrhea or obstipation suggesting autoimmune destruction of enterochromaffin(-like) cells
Chronic oral candidiasis with leukoplakia-like atrophic change carrying a risk of future carcinoma
harrison.prognosis: These are chronic, progressive disorders in which individual component diseases continue to emerge over years to decades, so cumulative prevalence rises with age and lifelong surveillance is required. APS-1 typically presents earliest (often infancy) and its chronic candidiasis is nearly always present and poorly responsive to treatment. In APS-2, autoantibodies can precede clinical disease by many years, allowing early detection; about half of patients with Addison's disease develop an additional autoimmune disorder over their lifetime, and individuals with two or more islet autoantibodies have a near-100% lifetime risk of clinical type 1 diabetes. With timely hormone replacement and monitoring, prognosis for individual endocrinopathies is generally favorable, but unrecognized adrenal insufficiency or precipitated adrenal crisis is potentially fatal (Harrison 22e p.3089-3091).
pitfalls: Initiating thyroid hormone before excluding/treating adrenal insufficiency, precipitating adrenal crisis
Failing to recognize that one component disorder warrants screening for others, and that siblings of an APS-1 patient should be considered affected even with a single component
Attributing chronic candidiasis purely to local infection rather than recognizing it as a marker of APS-1
Missing functional asplenism (Howell-Jolly bodies) in APS-1, which raises infection risk
Overlooking subclinical/preclinical disease detectable only by autoantibodies and physiologic testing
harrison.severityClassification: No formal severity grading is defined; classification is by type (APS-1 vs APS-2, with proposed APS-3/APS-4 subtypes) based on the constellation of component autoimmune disorders. For type 1 diabetes risk within APS-2, presence of two or more islet autoantibodies with normal glucose tolerance is staged as stage 1 disease (Harrison 22e p.3089-3091).
management: Hormone replacement tailored to each affected gland: glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid for Addison's disease, calcium and active vitamin D for hypoparathyroidism, levothyroxine for hypothyroidism and insulin for type 1 diabetes
Antifungal therapy with azoles for the chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis of APS-1
Immunosuppression for non-endocrine autoimmune manifestations where they arise
Adrenal crisis prevention with sick-day glucocorticoid rules and emergency parenteral hydrocortisone, commencing glucocorticoid before levothyroxine when adrenal and thyroid failure coexist
Lifelong surveillance for emerging component disorders, guided by organ-specific autoantibodies
Genetic counselling and family screening, particularly for autosomal-recessive AIRE-related APS-1
